posts.title: Why we grind every morning
posts.excerpt: Buckwheat flour loses its scent within a day. That is the whole reason the mill sits in the window.
posts.content:
Buckwheat flour starts to lose its scent the moment it leaves the stones. By the next day the grassy, nutty smell is half gone; by the end of the week it tastes of paper.

So we grind every opening morning, a few kilos at a time, and only as much as the day needs. When it is gone, it is gone. That is also why some days the noren comes down at one.

posts.title: Drink the soba-yu
posts.excerpt: The cloudy water in the square pitcher is the best part of the meal. Here is how to drink it.
posts.content:
When you finish a cold tray, a square wooden pitcher arrives. Inside is soba-yu, the water the noodles were boiled in, cloudy with buckwheat.

Pour it into what is left of your dipping broth, stir once and drink it warm. It softens the broth and carries the last of the flour’s taste.

posts.title: New crop in November
posts.excerpt: The first sacks of this year’s buckwheat come down from the farms in the first week of November.
posts.content:
The buckwheat on the two farms upriver flowered white in September and is being cut now. After drying it comes down in paper sacks, usually in the first week of November.

New-crop soba is greener and sweeter. For the first two weeks we serve it plain on the seiro, so you can taste the difference.

posts.title: Duck season
posts.excerpt: Kamo nanban returns with the first cool evenings: duck breast, leek grilled until sweet, and a darker broth.
posts.content:
When the evenings cool, the warm bowls change. Kamo nanban comes back: slices of duck breast, long pieces of leek grilled until they are sweet, and a broth made darker with the duck’s fat.

We make twelve bowls a day. When they are gone, today’s note says so.

posts.title: One point three millimetres
posts.excerpt: Why our soba is cut to 1.3 millimetres, and what a square knife and a guide board have to do with it.
posts.content:
A soba knife is square and heavy, and it never slices; it falls straight down. With each cut the guide board moves a hair to the side, and the width of the noodle is that hair.

We cut to 1.3 millimetres, a little thinner than most. Thin soba cools fast on the seiro and takes just enough broth.
